clinicalScope: Normal breast anatomy and clinical examination in adult women and adolescent females presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Breast Anatomy and Clinical Examination
subject: Anatomy
summary: The breast is a modified sweat gland on the anterior chest wall that produces milk and has important supportive and cosmetic roles. Understanding its development, structure, blood and nerve supply, and how to examine it is essential for clinicians in resource‑limited settings.

sections.p: The breast is a paired, superficial organ composed of glandular, fibrous, and adipose tissue that sits over the pectoralis major muscle. It functions primarily in lactation but also serves as a marker of hormonal status and a site for common pathology.
b: Modified sweat gland (apocrine) with milk‑producing alveoli
15–20 lobes per breast, each with lobules and ducts
Cooper’s ligaments provide structural support
Surrounded by variable adipose tissue influencing size

sections.p: Breast tissue originates from the ectodermal mammary ridge (milk line) that appears around the 4th week of gestation and regresses except at the thoracic level, where it forms the future breast bud.
b: Mammary ridge forms bilaterally from axilla to groin
Primary breast bud appears at the 6th week
Lobular differentiation begins at puberty under estrogen
Hormonal surge in pregnancy expands alveolar epithelium

sections.p: Each breast extends from the second to the sixth rib vertically and from the sternum to the mid‑axillary line horizontally. It lies superficial to the pectoralis major and deep to the skin and subcutaneous fat.
b: Superior border: clavicle; inferior border: 6th rib
Medial border: sternum; lateral border: mid‑axillary line
Retromammary (subglandular) space separates gland from pectoralis major
Nipple‑areolar complex centered over the fourth intercostal space

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the breast from three main sources, while venous drainage follows parallel pathways to the axillary and internal thoracic veins.
b: Medial mammary branches of internal thoracic artery (primary supply)
Lateral thoracic artery from axillary artery (supplementary supply)
Thoraco‑acromial (pectoral) branch and posterior intercostal arteries
Veins mirror arteries, draining mainly into axillary vein

sections.p: Sensory innervation derives from the intercostal nerves (T2‑T6) and the supraclavicular nerves; lymphatics follow predictable pathways to axillary and internal mammary nodes.
b: Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves T2‑T6
Supraclavicular nerves supply the upper pole
Lymph drains to level I‑III axillary nodes (most clinically relevant)
Medial drainage to internal mammary nodes via perforating branches

sections.p: The breast consists of a ductal‑lobular system embedded in a fibrous‑adipose stroma. The epithelium is lined by two layers of cells that respond to hormonal cues.
b: Lobules contain alveoli lined by secretory cuboidal cells and myoepithelial cells
Lactiferous ducts lined by columnar luminal cells and basal myoepithelial cells
Cooper’s ligaments are dense collagen bundles
Montgomery tubercles are sebaceous glands on the areola

sections.p: Beyond milk production, the breast provides tactile feedback, contributes to body image, and its connective framework resists gravitational ptosis.
b: Alveolar cells synthesize milk under prolactin stimulation
Oxytocin‑mediated myoepithelial contraction expels milk
Cooper’s ligaments maintain shape; loss leads to sagging
Adipose layer determines size and protects underlying tissue

sections.p: Knowledge of breast anatomy guides procedures such as clinical examination, fine‑needle aspiration, and mastectomy, and helps predict spread of infection or tumour.
b: Location of axillary nodes predicts metastatic pathways
Retromammary space is a potential site for abscesses or implants
Understanding ductal layout aids in nipple discharge localisation
Cooper’s ligaments tether the skin; retraction suggests underlying fibrosis or tumour

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the most frequent breast problems are mastitis, abscess formation, and benign fibro‑adenoma; traumatic rupture of Cooper’s ligaments can cause dimpling.
b: Acute puerperal mastitis: bacterial infection of lactating breast
Sub‑areolar abscess: often Staphylococcus aureus, may require drainage
Fibro‑adenoma: firm, mobile mass common in adolescents
Traumatic ligament rupture → skin dimpling, mimics malignancy

sections.p: Physical examination remains primary; when available, ultrasound is the first imaging modality, while mammography is limited by cost and equipment.
b: Inspection: symmetry, skin changes, nipple retraction
Palpation: circular motion, assess for masses, tenderness, lymph nodes
Ultrasound: distinguishes cystic from solid lesions, guides FNAC
If ultrasound unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and refer if suspicious

sections.p: Normal variation includes size, shape, and degree of ptosis. Congenital anomalies such as polythelia (extra nipples) or accessory breast tissue can be mistaken for pathology.
b: Polymastia: accessory breast tissue along milk line
Polythelia: supernumerary nipples, usually benign
Tubular breasts: congenital hypoplasia, may affect lactation
Asymmetry >1 cm warrants further evaluation

sections.p: A systematic bedside exam ensures no finding is missed and respects patient modesty, crucial in culturally sensitive settings.
b: Introduce self, obtain consent, ensure chaperone, patient seated with arms relaxed
Inspect with arms at sides, raised, then supine; note contour, skin, nipple
Palpate using pads of fingers in concentric circles, assess all quadrants and axilla
Document any mass size, consistency, mobility, skin changes, and discharge

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with fever suggesting abscess

faq.q: Why is the axillary lymph node group most important in breast disease?
faq.a: It is the first drainage basin for most breast tissue and the site where metastatic cancer cells first lodge.

faq.q: Can a breast abscess be managed without imaging?
faq.a: Yes, if clinical signs of fluctuation and systemic infection are clear; drainage can be performed empirically, but ultrasound helps confirm.

faq.q: What is the purpose of the retromammary space?
faq.a: It allows breast movement over the chest wall and can accommodate fluid collections or implants.

exam: A 19‑year‑old woman presents with a firm, mobile 2 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant; what is your next step and why? — Perform focused breast ultrasound to differentiate cystic from solid lesion before deciding on FNAC.
During a routine exam you note skin dimpling over a 3 cm mass; which structure is likely involved and what does this suggest? — Involvement of Cooper’s ligaments; raises suspicion for malignancy.

A lactating mother has a tender, erythematous breast with a fluctuant area; what investigations are essential in a low‑resource setting? — Clinical assessment; if possible, bedside ultrasound to locate abscess; otherwise proceed to incision and drainage.

Explain how the internal thoracic artery contributes to breast blood supply and why this matters in mastectomy. — It supplies the medial breast; ligation is required to control intra‑operative bleeding.

A patient reports unilateral nipple discharge that is clear and milky; what anatomical pathway should you examine and why? — Follow the lactiferous ducts centrally to the subareolar region; discharge often originates from ductal ectasia or papilloma.

What are the key differences between fibro‑adenoma and a malignant tumour on physical exam? — Fibro‑adenoma is usually well‑circumscribed, mobile, and painless; malignancy may be fixed, irregular, and associated with skin changes.

In a setting without mammography, how would you screen a high‑risk woman for early breast cancer? — Perform thorough clinical breast exam every 6‑12 months and use ultrasound if a suspicious lesion is felt.
Why is it important to assess the contralateral breast during examination? — Bilateral comparison helps identify subtle asymmetry and reduces missed pathology.
A newborn female has palpable breast tissue; is this normal and what is the usual management? — Physiologic neonatal breast enlargement due to maternal hormones; reassurance and observation only.
During a mastectomy you encounter a thickened retromammary fascia; what is its clinical relevance? — It may contain residual breast tissue; careful removal reduces local recurrence risk.
